q: Functionalism, an early school of thought in psychology, was most closely associated with which psychologist?

concept.t: Functionalism asked what the mind is for: how mental processes help us adapt, not what they are made of.
James's Principles of Psychology (1890) inspired the question; Dewey and Angell made it a formal school at Chicago.

wrong.a: Founded structuralism, the rival school that broke the mind into its elements by introspection.
wrong.b: Founded behaviourism (1913), which dropped the mind and studied only behaviour.
wrong.d: Functionalist in spirit, but examined for institutions such as the first American research laboratory (1883) and the APA (1892).

q: The first person to use the term clinical psychology in print was

concept.t: Witmer opened the first psychological clinic at the University of Pennsylvania in 1896.
He used the term clinical psychology in print in his journal The Psychological Clinic (1907).

wrong.a: Known for the psychosocial stages, not for naming clinical psychology.
wrong.b: Known for psychoanalysis, not for naming clinical psychology.
wrong.d: James McKeen Cattell is known for coining "mental test", not clinical psychology.

q: Match List I with List II LIST I (Psychologist) LIST 2 (Theory) A. Dollard and Miller 1. Radical Behaviorism B. Skinner 2. Self-Actualization C. Bandura and Walters 3. Early Social Learning D. Maslow 4. Later Social Learning
who: Dollard and Miller (1950); Bandura and Walters (1963)

concept.t: Dollard and Miller recast Freud in Hull's terms in 1950: early social learning (A-3).
Bandura and Walters gave the later social learning theory (1963), built on observation and modelling (C-4).
Skinner's system is radical behaviourism (B-1); Maslow is self-actualisation (D-2).

wrong.a: Gets every pair wrong: Dollard and Miller are not radical behaviourism, Skinner is not self-actualisation, and the two social learning labels are swapped.
wrong.c: Only B-1 is right; Dollard and Miller are not self-actualisation, Bandura and Walters are later (not early) social learning, and Maslow is not social learning.
wrong.d: Gets A and C right but swaps Skinner and Maslow; it tempts only if you forget that Skinner, not Maslow, is the radical behaviourist.

q: Which is the correct order of the last four of Patanjali's eight limbs?

concept.t: The senses are first withdrawn inward (pratyahara), then the mind is fixed on one point (dharana).
The fixing becomes an unbroken flow (dhyana) and finally absorption (samadhi).
Each wrong option swaps two of these steps; remember the order withdraw, fix, flow, absorb.

wrong.a: Swaps the first two: pratyahara (withdrawing the senses) must come before dharana (fixing the mind).
wrong.c: Swaps the middle two: dharana (fixing on one point) must come before dhyana, its unbroken flow.
wrong.d: Swaps the first and third: it starts with dhyana, but sense withdrawal (pratyahara) comes first.

q: Which statement is INCORRECT?
who: Rods versus cones in the retina

concept.t: Cones, with three pigments, give colour vision, so they are not monochromatic.
It is the rods, with one pigment (rhodopsin), that give colourless scotopic vision.

wrong.a: True: cones are packed in the fovea, at the centre of the retina.
wrong.b: True: cones work in moderate to bright light, while the rods handle dim light.
wrong.d: True: cones give excellent acuity, sharpest in the fovea where they are packed.

q: In signal detection theory, the ability to distinguish a stimulus from background noise is:

concept.t: d′ is the separation between the noise and signal-plus-noise distributions.
It does not depend on the observer's willingness to say "yes", so it measures the ability to detect alone.

wrong.b: The observer's willingness to say "yes" (response bias), not the ability to detect.
wrong.c: A graph that plots hit rate against false alarm rate, not the ability itself.
wrong.d: The just noticeable difference belongs to classical psychophysics, not signal detection theory.

q: Among monocular cues for depth perception is

concept.t: In interposition, an object that partly hides another is seen as nearer.
One eye is enough to see the overlap, so it is a monocular cue.

wrong.a: A binocular cue (the eyes turn inward for near objects); convergence and retinal disparity are the only two binocular cues.
wrong.b: The other binocular cue: each eye gets a slightly different image, so it needs both eyes.
wrong.c: Not a depth cue at all; it is Piaget's term for fitting new experience into existing schemas.

q: Illusions are

concept.t: In an illusion a real external stimulus is present but is misread.
Contrast a hallucination, which is perception without an adequate external stimulus.

wrong.b: A sensory distortion such as micropsia, where a real object looks changed (smaller).
wrong.c: Imagery, produced by the mind with no stimulus being misread.
wrong.d: The definition of a hallucination, not an illusion.

q: The Stroop effect demonstrates interference in

concept.t: Word reading is automatic, so it cannot be filtered out while naming the ink colour.
The task therefore shows a failure of selective attention.

wrong.a: A memory distractor: no stored memory is being retrieved from long-term memory.
wrong.b: A memory distractor: nothing is being rehearsed in working memory; the clash is in attention.
wrong.d: A memory distractor: procedural memory is skill memory, and no stored skill is being retrieved here.

q: According to Freud, the ___ mind includes accessible memories, which can be recalled at will
who: Freud's topographical model of the mind

concept.t: Freud's preconscious holds memories outside current awareness that can be recalled at will.
The conscious holds only what is in awareness now; the unconscious cannot be recalled at will.

wrong.a: Holds only what is in awareness now, not stored memories waiting to be recalled.
wrong.c: Its contents cannot be recalled at will, so it does not fit "accessible memories".
wrong.d: A principle (no mental event is accidental), not a level of mind.

q: Systematic desensitization technique is based upon the idea of:

concept.t: Wolpe paired each step of an anxiety hierarchy with relaxation.
Relaxation is a response incompatible with anxiety, so the anxiety bond weakens: reciprocal inhibition.

wrong.b: Thorndike's operant principle: behaviour followed by satisfaction is strengthened.
wrong.c: Underlies exposure and response prevention, which uses no competing response such as relaxation.
wrong.d: Belongs to stress theory, not to the learning principle behind desensitization.

q: Among the following schedules of reinforcement, which typically produces the highest rate of response and is most resistant to extinction?

concept.t: Ratio schedules reward fast responding: the more responses, the more reinforcers.
Unpredictability removes any reason to pause and makes it hard to tell that reinforcement has stopped, as with slot machines.

wrong.a: Fast too, but shows a pause after each reinforcer and gives up sooner in extinction, since the end of reward is easier to spot.
wrong.c: Produces a scallop: little responding just after a reinforcer, speeding up as the next one nears.
wrong.d: Gives only a moderate, steady rate, because responding faster does not earn reinforcement sooner.

q: The famous patient H.M. (Henry Molaison) underwent surgical removal of the medial temporal lobes, including the hippocampus, to treat severe epilepsy. While he retained most of his intellectual abilities and working memory, his primary and most profound deficit was in:

concept.t: After the 1953 operation H.M. could not form new declarative memories: a profound anterograde amnesia.
His intelligence, digit span and childhood memories survived.

wrong.a: Spared: he learned mirror tracing, improving with practice though he did not remember the sessions.
wrong.b: Old semantic knowledge was intact; his loss was in forming new memories.
wrong.d: Present but limited: his retrograde amnesia covered only the years before surgery.

q: Which of the following terms refers to difficulty recalling information due to interference from new information?

concept.t: In retroactive interference, new learning reaches back to disrupt older memories.
RETRO: new disrupts old, acting backwards in time.

wrong.b: The reverse: old learning disrupts new learning.
wrong.c: Decay blames the passage of time, not competition from new learning.
wrong.d: Retrieval failure blames a mismatch of cues, not competition from new learning.

q: In which method does the researcher gather data, look for patterns, and then generate a theory or hypothesis?
who: Inductive reasoning: data first, theory last

concept.t: Induction runs from specific observations to a probable generalisation.
Data come first and theory last, as in most qualitative research.

wrong.a: Deduction runs the other way, from a theory to a tested prediction.
wrong.b: Also runs from a theory to a tested prediction: form a hypothesis, deduce a result, then test it.
wrong.d: Abduction infers the best explanation of a surprising fact, rather than generalising from patterns.

q: What is the primary difference between Piaget and Vygotsky's theories of language development?
who: Piaget versus Vygotsky on thought and language

concept.t: For Piaget, language expresses concepts already built through action, so language depends on thought.
For Vygotsky, thought and speech merge at about two, after which thought becomes verbal and depends on language.

wrong.a: Swaps the names: it is Vygotsky, not Piaget, who made thought depend on language.
wrong.c: False: both studied the same preschool years.
wrong.d: Fails because (b) states the difference correctly.

q: The term IQ was invented by

concept.t: Stern proposed the intelligence quotient in 1912: mental age divided by chronological age.
Terman multiplied the quotient by 100 and popularised it in the 1916 Stanford-Binet, but did not coin it.

wrong.a: Terman is the tempting wrong answer: he popularised the IQ but did not coin it.
wrong.b: Allport is known for traits; he never worked on the IQ.
wrong.d: Watson is known for behaviourism; he never worked on the IQ.

q: A 10-year-old child from a rural area, with no formal schooling, is brought for an intellectual assessment due to academic struggles. The child is illiterate and has had minimal exposure to formal testing materials. Which of the following tests would be the MOST appropriate to use to minimize cultural and educational bias?

concept.t: Its five performance subtests need no reading, so an illiterate child is not penalised.
It has Indian rural norms, which fit a rural child with no formal schooling.

wrong.b: Rests on school-built verbal knowledge and foreign norms, so it is biased against this child.
wrong.c: The SB5 also rests on school-built verbal knowledge and foreign norms.
wrong.d: The tempting Indian option, but half of it is verbal, adapted from the WISC.

q: The ‘satiety centre’ of the brain is located in the:

concept.t: Bilateral VMH lesions make rats overeat and grow obese (Hetherington and Ranson, 1940).
So Stellar's dual-centre theory (1954) called the ventromedial hypothalamus the satiety centre.

wrong.a: The opposite, the feeding centre: its destruction causes aphagia (Anand and Brobeck, 1951).
wrong.b: Invented by changing one word; the hippocampus serves memory, not satiety.
wrong.c: Invented by changing one word; the thalamus is a sensory relay, not a hunger centre.

q: According to Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, which of the following factors are considered motivators that lead to job satisfaction?

concept.t: Herzberg's motivators lie in the content of the work: achievement, recognition, the work itself, responsibility, advancement and growth.
Hygiene factors prevent dissatisfaction when good but do not by themselves motivate.

wrong.a: Salary and benefits are hygiene factors: good pay prevents dissatisfaction but does not by itself motivate.
wrong.b: Job security and working conditions are hygiene factors, part of the setting rather than the content of the work.
wrong.d: Company policies and relationships are hygiene factors; good ones prevent dissatisfaction but do not motivate.

q: The seat of emotion is to be found in _________________.

concept.t: MacLean's limbic system (1952), built on Papez's circuit, is the classic seat of emotion.
It includes the amygdala, central to fear and emotional learning.

wrong.b: Paces heartbeat and breathing, basic life functions rather than emotion.
wrong.d: Too broad: the limbic system lies within the forebrain, but so does much else.

q: 'Psychological disorders develop when a biological predisposition is set off by a stressful situation', is proposed by

concept.t: A pre-existing vulnerability (diathesis) set off by a stressful trigger (stress) is the model's definition.
Meehl (1962) and Zubin and Spring (1977) set out the model.

wrong.a: Humanistic-existential models blame blocked growth, not predisposition plus stress.
wrong.b: Sociocultural models blame social forces, not a biological predisposition.
wrong.d: Cognitive models blame faulty thinking; none is defined by predisposition plus stress.
